title: Integers, factors, multiples, primes, squares and roots
blurb: Work with negative numbers, find factors, multiples, primes, the GCF and the LCM, and use perfect squares to find and estimate square roots.
question: One patient's dressing is changed every 6 days and another's every 8 days, and both were changed today. In how many days will both fall on the same day again, and is that the GCF or the LCM of 6 and 8?

teach.body: Formally, integers are the whole numbers and their opposites (…, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, …); a factor of a number divides it evenly, a multiple is the number times a whole number, a prime has exactly two factors (1 and itself), and a square root √a is the nonnegative number whose square is a. In plain English: learn a few sign rules, know your times tables backward and forward, and memorize the perfect squares to 225.

head: Situation
Rule
Example
rows: Subtract sizes; sign of larger size
teach.caption: "Size" means absolute value, the distance from 0: |−7| = 7. On a number line, −2 > −5.
Several factors: an even number of negatives gives a positive, an odd number a negative.
Two numbers' product (6 × 8 = 48) is a common multiple, but not always the least.
Read the grid backward for square roots: √196 = 14.

items: √50 is not a perfect square. Find the neighbors: 49 < 50 < 64, so 7 < √50 < 8.
50 is much closer to 49 than to 64, so √50 is just above 7 (about 7.07).
Decimal roots: √0.49 = 0.7, because 0.7 × 0.7 = 0.49 (2 decimal places in the square, 1 in the root).

teach.text: Number-fact slips the HESI A2 uses: calling 1 prime (it is neither) or 51 and 91 prime (both composite); swapping the GCF and LCM; treating 2³ as 2 × 3; reading −3² as 9 (it is −9; only (−3)² = 9); and ordering negatives by size, as if −8 were greater than −2.

teach.h: Scenario: Rosa plans a schedule and kits
teach.body: Rosa Martinez, a nursing applicant working as a unit clerk, sees one dressing changed every 6 days and another every 8 days. Multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24; multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24. The LCM is 24, so both fall together in 24 days. She also packs 24 gauze pads and 36 tape strips into identical kits with nothing left over: the GCF of 24 and 36 is 12, so 12 kits of 2 pads and 3 strips.

items: Same signs add and keep the sign; subtracting a negative is adding.
× and ÷: same signs positive, different signs negative.
1 is neither prime nor composite; 2 is the only even prime.
GCF ≤ the smaller number (simplifying); LCM ≥ the larger number (schedules, common denominators).
Know the squares to 15² = 225 and estimate other roots between neighbors.

summary: You can now add, subtract, multiply and divide negative numbers with the right sign, test divisibility, sort primes from composites, and find the GCF and LCM. You also know the perfect squares to 225 and use them to find and estimate square roots.

A.q: What is the greatest common factor of 36 and 60?
A.why: Factors of 36: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36. Factors of 60 include 12 but not 18 or 36. The greatest shared factor is 12.

whyNot.1: 6 is a common factor, but not the greatest; 12 also divides both.
whyNot.2: 180 is the least common multiple, not the greatest common factor.
whyNot.3: 2,160 is the product 36 × 60, a common multiple.

A.q: Between which two consecutive whole numbers does √130 lie?

whyNot.0: 10² = 100 and 11² = 121, both less than 130, so √130 is above 11.
whyNot.1: 12² = 144 is already more than 130, so √130 is below 12.
whyNot.2: 121 and 144 are the perfect squares around 130; the roots are their square roots, 11 and 12.

B.why: (−2)(−5) = 10; 10 × (−3) = −30; −30 ÷ (−6) = 5. Four negatives (an even count) give a positive result.

whyNot.0: −5 gets the sign wrong: there are four negative numbers, an even count, so the result is positive.
whyNot.2: −30 is the product of the first three numbers, before dividing by −6.

B.q: Which number is divisible by both 3 and 4?
B.why: 348: digit sum 3 + 4 + 8 = 15, divisible by 3; last two digits 48, divisible by 4. (348 = 12 × 29.)

whyNot.0: 134 fails both tests: digit sum 8, and 34 is not divisible by 4.
whyNot.1: 222 passes the 3 test (digit sum 6) but 22 is not divisible by 4.
whyNot.2: 316 passes the 4 test (16 ÷ 4 = 4) but its digit sum, 10, is not divisible by 3.

C.q: Two IV pumps need checks, one every 12 minutes and one every 18 minutes. Both are checked at 9:00 a.m. When are both next due at the same time?
C.why: The next shared time is the LCM of 12 and 18. Multiples of 18: 18, 36; 36 is also a multiple of 12. LCM = 36 minutes, so 9:36 a.m.

whyNot.0: 9:06 adds the GCF of 12 and 18 (6), not the LCM.
whyNot.1: 9:30 adds the two intervals (12 + 18); the checks meet at a common multiple.
whyNot.2: 12:36 p.m. adds 12 × 18 = 216 minutes, a common multiple but not the least.

C.why: Exponent and root first: 2² = 4 and √36 = 6. Multiply: 4 × 6 = 24. Then 5 + 24 − (−4) = 29 + 4 = 33.

whyNot.0: √64 + √36 = 8 + 6 = 14, but √100 = 10. The square root of a sum cannot be split.
whyNot.1: (−5)² = (−5)(−5) = 25; the parentheses include the negative in the square.
whyNot.2: 1 has only one factor, so it is neither prime nor composite.

reteach.title: Think like a thermometer
reteach.question: On a winter morning the thermometer reads −5°F. It warms up 12 degrees, then drops 15 degrees. How does reading a thermometer make the sign rules obvious?

blocks.h: Up is plus, down is minus
blocks.body: A thermometer is a number line standing up. Adding moves you up, subtracting moves you down. Start at −5 and warm up 12: you pass 0 after 5 degrees and keep going 7 more, landing on 7. Drop 15: you fall 7 degrees to 0 and 8 more, landing on −8. Subtracting a negative is like a cold front being canceled: removing a drop makes it warmer.

items: −5 + 12: different signs, 12 − 5 = 7, larger size is positive: 7.
7 − 15: same as 7 + (−15); different signs, 15 − 7 = 8, larger size is negative: −8.
The thermometer and the rules agree. ✓

blocks.text: −8 is colder than −5. On a number line, the farther left (or lower), the smaller the number.

explain.body: Change every subtraction to adding the opposite, then combine. Same signs: add sizes, keep the sign. Different signs: subtract sizes, keep the sign of the larger size.

test.why: − (−9) = + 9, so −15 + 9 + 4 = −15 + 13. Sizes: 15 − 13 = 2, and the larger size (15) is negative: −2.

whyNot.2: 2 gets the size right but takes the sign of the smaller size; 15 is larger and negative.
whyNot.3: −28 treats both the − (−9) and the + 4 as subtractions.

explain.body: Same signs give a positive, different signs give a negative. For a chain, count the negatives: even count positive, odd count negative.

whyNot.0: −3 has the wrong sign: dividing a negative by a negative gives a positive.
whyNot.1: −24 is the product before dividing by −8, an intermediate step.

explain.body: A prime has exactly two factors, 1 and itself. 1 is neither prime nor composite, and 2 is the only even prime. To test a number, try the primes whose squares are not bigger than it.

test.q: Which list contains only prime numbers?
test.why: 2, 3, 5 and 7 each have exactly two factors: 1 and the number itself.

whyNot.1: 1 has only one factor, so it is not prime.
whyNot.2: 9 = 3 × 3 has three factors, so it is composite.
whyNot.3: 51 = 3 × 17 is composite (its digit sum, 6, is divisible by 3).

explain.body: Find the perfect squares on either side. √75: 64 < 75 < 81, so between 8 and 9. 75 is closer to 81 (6 away) than to 64 (11 away), so the root is a little over 8.5.

test.q: Which is the best estimate of √75?
test.why: 64 < 75 < 81, so √75 is between 8 and 9, nearer 9. Check: 8.7² = 75.69, very close to 75.

whyNot.0: 7.5 just moves the decimal point in 75; 7.5² = 56.25.
whyNot.1: 8.3 leans toward 8, but 75 is closer to 81 than to 64; 8.3² = 68.89.
whyNot.3: 9.3 is above 9, but 9² = 81 is already more than 75.
